newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NAB says govt block on bank mergers myopic.
newsitem.headline: NAB says govt block on bank mergers myopic.

text.p: National Australia Bank (NAB) Managing Director Don Argus attacked the government's block on big bank mergers, saying on Friday it was a myopic and farcical attempt to hold off industry rationalisation.
Argus also said the government's encouragement of foreign bank takeovers of local banks to boost competition was based on a fallacious assumption.
Argus told an Institute of Chartered Accountants function in Adelaide that broad-based reform of Australia's banking and financial system had stalled.
"In the case of banking, the situation is complicated by the fact that not only is reform stalled, but there is a lack of clarity regarding the intent and basis of governemnt policy," he said.
Australia could not isolate itself from the global trend towards larger and more complex international banking and financial groups, he said.
"To date, the federal government has come up with the curious response of encouraging foreign takeovers of Australian banks, but prohibiting Australian takeovers of Australian banks," Argus said.
"This is based on the fallacious assumption that a foreign takeover of a local bank would encourage competition because a foreign bank would automatically force local prices lower."

This overlooked the likelihood that Australian banks would now only be taken over for a high price and a foreign bank-local bank merger would not achieve the same efficiency gains as the merger of two local banks, Argus said.
A foreign takeover of a local bank would result in efficiency gains of up to 30 percent below those possible from an in-market merger, he said.

"So we have this farcical situation where in the interests of greater competition and efficiency, the federal government is encouraging a takeover option that is guaranteed to achieve a relatively lower level of potential merger benefits," he said.
National Australia Bank had no problem with takeovers by foreign banks as such, he said.
"What we find absolutely extraordinary is the fact that an Australian company such as the National cannot bid for another bank here, but foreign banks are positively encouraged to do so."
While the Australian industry was waiting to be rationalised, other countries like Germany and the Netherlands were encouraging such rationalisation, he said.
"Eventually the penny will drop, if you are under-capitalised, your long term future cannot be guaranteed," Argus said. These realities had been overlooked by some in government, he said.
"This is nonsense and the Wallis Committee members have rightly said so."

Commonwealth Bank of Australia managing director David Murray warned in April that the proposals by the government's Wallis Financial System Inquiry to strip the Reserve Bank of Australia of its prudential powers created the risk of Savings & Loan-style collapses.
NAB is at loggerheads with the three other major banks, ANZ Banking Group Ltd, Westpac Banking Corp and CBA over prudential and systemic reform.
NAB wants a more laissez faire approach that opens up the market to competition from non-banks and allows big bank mergers.
The other three want the Reserve Bank to keep its prudential power and have not argued so strongly for big-bank mergers.

NAB is seen the most likely predator if big-bank mergers are allowed by the government, which said in April when it released the Wallis report it wanted to see more competition develop before releasing the shackles.
Westpac and ANZ are seen the most likely takeover targets.
